strengths: The hybrid representation is a meaningful and well-motivated contribution: vectorized object primitives provide compact, instance-addressable geometry, while raster maps accommodate irregular ground surfaces. This directly enables object translation, rotation, scaling, and modality-specific latent manipulation that are cumbersome with voxels.

The method is technically coherent and described in substantial detail. The manuscript specifies the VAE and DiT architectures, matching losses, category-dependent query counts and weights, optimization settings, dataset construction, and inpainting/outpainting procedure, supporting reasonable reproducibility.

The Cholesky parameterization is an interesting way to remove irrelevant sign ambiguities when jointly encoding box orientation and scale. The controlled synthetic experiment uses nested training sets, a shared test set, and five random seeds, and consistently favors Cholesky encoding over the quaternion regression baseline.

The quantitative generation results are large and consistent across the reported metrics: DiT-B improves FID from 156.241 to 55.041 and precision/recall from 0.0288/0.0472 to 0.4532/0.4360 relative to SemCity. Additional sampling configurations in the supplement preserve the substantial precision/recall advantage.

The qualitative results are clear and extensive. They illustrate plausible primitive layouts, vegetation conditioning, ground-conditioned object generation, localized editing, and iterative scene extension; the paper also candidly shows floating-object and incoherent-outpainting failures.
weaknesses: The central comparison is not sufficiently controlled to support the strength of the claimed generative advantage. SemCity completes only 18 epochs in the same wall-clock period in which the proposed VAE completes 300, and no convergence curves, compute-matched alternatives, or evidence that the SemCity diffusion baseline is adequately optimized are provided. This is especially concerning because SemCity's reported generation precision and recall are extremely low despite its high-resolution autoencoder attaining substantially better reconstruction than PrITTI.

The memory-efficiency conclusion is selectively framed. PrITTI uses 2.52 MB and obtains 70.27 mIoU, whereas the 1.00 MB SemCity representation obtains 68.98 mIoU; the claimed over-3x saving instead compares against an 8.00 MB configuration attaining 93.81 mIoU, which is not similar reconstruction quality. Moreover, the hybrid method remains resolution-dependent through its 256x256, ten-channel ground raster, so the statement that the representation is resolution-independent is inaccurate.

Evaluation breadth is limited to one dataset and principally one voxel baseline. The scarcity of primitive annotations explains the dataset limitation, but comparisons or adapted experiments against related vectorized driving-layout generators and 2.5D city-layout methods would help separate the benefit of primitives from architecture, training, and rendering choices.

The headline controllability and downstream-application claims are supported almost entirely qualitatively. There is no measurement of vegetation-label adherence, preservation of known regions during inpainting, boundary continuity or long-range consistency during outpainting, collision rates, road-object compatibility, or human assessment of plausibility. The photo-realistic examples additionally rely on an externally trained ControlNet and therefore provide little evidence about PrITTI itself.

The generative metrics are computed by applying Inception features to top-down semantic renderings. Such features are designed for natural RGB images and can respond strongly to representation-specific contours and rendering appearance; this may inherently favor clean primitives over voxel renderings. No representation-neutral structural metrics or downstream utility evaluation corroborate the reported FID/IS results.

The purportedly overlap-minimizing split excludes poses within only 5 m even though every sample covers a 64 m x 64 m region. Consequently, train and test layouts can still share substantial physical scene content, weakening the interpretation of held-out reconstruction results.

Some reproducibility-critical details remain absent or ambiguous, including code availability, exact normalization and inversion of Cholesky parameters, random seeds for the main experiments, and variability across diffusion training runs. The manuscript also reports no uncertainty for its main quantitative comparisons.

strengths: The hybrid representation is well motivated: vectorized object primitives provide compact, instance-addressable geometry, while raster maps accommodate irregular ground surfaces. This is a useful direction for controllable urban-layout generation.

The manuscript presents a coherent end-to-end system, including a set-based object VAE, a structured ground/object latent, latent diffusion, and manipulation through inpainting and direct primitive transformations.

The reported generation results substantially outperform the implemented SemCity baseline on all four image-based metrics; for example, DiT-B improves FID from 156.24 to 55.04 and precision from 0.0288 to 0.4532 while reducing reported sampling time.

The paper includes useful implementation details, dataset construction procedures, representation ablations, failure cases, and compute information. The qualitative examples demonstrate diverse layouts and make the editing interface easy to understand.
weaknesses: The principal comparison does not convincingly isolate the benefit of primitives. PrITTI and SemCity use materially different autoencoders and generative pipelines, and SemCity's autoencoder completes only 18 epochs in the three-day budget versus 300 epochs for PrITTI. There is no convergence-matched comparison or adaptation of a vectorized driving-layout generator. Consequently, the large generation gap could reflect architecture, optimization, or an undertrained baseline rather than the proposed representation.

The generation evaluation is weak for the central 3D semantic-layout claims. FID, Inception Score, precision, and recall are computed from top-down color-coded semantic renderings using image features designed for natural images. These metrics do not assess 3D geometry, collisions, object-ground consistency, class/count distributions, or road adherence. The authors also show that precision varies dramatically with their sampling threshold and neighborhood size, making the headline numbers protocol-dependent.

The controllability and downstream claims receive almost entirely qualitative support. There is no measurement of whether generated scenes attain the requested vegetation level, no preservation or boundary-consistency metric for inpainting/outpainting, no user evaluation, and no quantitative assessment of ground-conditioned object placement. Direct rotation, scaling, and translation are representation operations rather than learned editing capabilities.

The reconstruction evidence conflicts with the strongest efficiency framing. At the common 256x256x32 evaluation resolution, PrITTI obtains 70.27 mIoU, substantially below SemCity's 93.81. It only slightly exceeds the 128-resolution baseline's 68.98 mIoU while using 2.52 MB rather than 1.00 MB. Moreover, the memory comparison depends on particular dense datatypes and excludes sparse or compressed voxel storage; the full hybrid representation is not resolution-independent because its ground component is a fixed 256x256 raster.

The Cholesky contribution is insufficiently validated. Its only comparison is a synthetic, zero-centered, yaw-only single-vehicle experiment against naive quaternion regression. Quaternion sign ambiguity has standard canonicalization or sign-invariant-loss remedies, and established continuous rotation encodings are not compared. The experiment therefore does not establish that Cholesky parameterization is preferable for the actual multi-object 3D task.

The reconstruction protocol leaves important gaps: AP excludes vegetation ellipsoids despite their being one of the two dominant primitive categories, reports no per-class performance, uses unusually low IoU thresholds in its averaged AP, and provides no uncertainty across training runs. The custom split also excludes poses only within 5 m even though each sample covers a 64 m field of view, so substantial train-test scene overlap may remain.

Evaluation is restricted to one dataset and mostly one baseline. This limitation is understandable given annotation availability, but together with the baseline and metric issues it prevents the manuscript from adequately supporting broad claims of superior generation quality, scalability, and usefulness for simulation. Reproducibility is further limited by the absence of an explicit code/model release commitment.

The empirical gains over SemCity are substantial: DiT-B improves FID from 156.241 to 55.041, precision from 0.0288 to 0.4532, and recall from 0.0472 to 0.4360, while reducing reported sampling time from 2.35 s to 0.58 s. The gains persist across alternative precision/recall evaluation configurations.

The Cholesky parameterization is a sensible geometry-aware way to remove irrelevant sign symmetries while jointly encoding scale and orientation. The five-seed synthetic study supports improved stability over direct quaternion regression.

The ablations provide useful evidence for the split latent design: removing the split degrades primitive AP3D from 62.12 to 53.78 and substantially worsens ground reconstruction. Joint ground/object training also modestly improves primitive reconstruction over an object-only model.

The work demonstrates a broad and practically attractive capability set—conditional generation, instance editing, inpainting, iterative outpainting, ground-conditioned object synthesis, and downstream street-view rendering—without task-specific retraining for the layout operations.

The manuscript is clear and unusually forthcoming about metric sensitivity and failure modes. The supplement documents data construction, architecture, loss weights, optimization settings, several evaluation configurations, and limitations such as floating objects and inconsistent outpainting.
weaknesses: The main comparison does not isolate the benefit of the representation from differences in the generative pipeline. PrITTI uses a DiT with up to 675M parameters, whereas only one voxel-generation system is evaluated under its own architecture. SemCity also completes only 18 autoencoder epochs in the three-day budget versus 300 for PrITTI. This is a legitimate efficiency result, but it weakens the stronger causal claim that primitives themselves explain the generation-quality gap.

Generation is evaluated mainly after converting scenes into 2D top-down semantic images and applying Inception-based metrics. These measures do not directly assess 3D geometry, collisions, object-ground support, topology, or semantic plausibility; their pronounced sensitivity to sample count and neighborhood size, documented by the authors, further limits the conclusiveness of the absolute numbers.

Evidence for controllability and downstream applications is almost entirely qualitative. There is no quantitative condition-adherence test for vegetation density, no preservation or seam-consistency metric for inpainting/outpainting, and no physical-validity or user evaluation for edited layouts. Thus, these capabilities are convincing demonstrations but not yet rigorously characterized.

The claimed memory advantage requires qualification. Of the reported 2.52 MB, 2.50 MB is a fixed 256×256 raster, so the hybrid representation is not fully resolution-independent as stated. The comparison also measures stored scene representations rather than peak training/inference memory, and the fixed object-query budget discards instances above each category's 95th-percentile count.

The Cholesky study compares only against naive quaternion regression on a simple synthetic, single-object yaw task. It does not compare with canonicalized quaternions or established continuous rotation representations, nor demonstrate an end-to-end benefit on real KITTI-360 scenes, so the claimed superiority is narrower than the presentation suggests.

There is a likely indexing error or insufficiently specified implementation detail in the inpainting derivation: the known sample denoted z_(t-1) is drawn using alpha-bar_t rather than alpha-bar_(t-1). Clarification is needed to determine whether this is only a presentation mistake or affects the sampler.

Evaluation is limited to one dataset and one principal baseline. The dataset scarcity makes this understandable and should not by itself determine rejection, but it restricts evidence for generalization beyond KITTI-360 and for superiority over other vectorized layout or driving-scene generators.

strengths: The hybrid representation—vectorized instance-level primitives for objects plus rasterized ground surfaces—is well motivated and materially improves editability and compactness over fully voxelized layouts. Direct object translation, rotation, scaling, and removal are natural consequences of the representation rather than post-hoc additions.

The method is technically coherent: a set-based Transformer encoder, spatial scatter operation, DETR-style decoder, disentangled ground/object latent channels, and latent diffusion model form a sensible end-to-end design. The Cholesky parameterization provides a compact, symmetry-aware joint encoding of orientation and extent.

The empirical gains in generation are large and consistent across the reported metrics. DiT-B reaches precision/recall of 0.712/0.491 and FID 73.952, versus 0.482/0.230 and FID 94.822 for the strongest XCube baseline, while also reducing reported sampling time from 3.50 s to 0.58 s.

The baseline study is broader than a single comparison: SemCity, PDD, and XCube are retrained on the same voxelized data, hierarchical levels are separately reported, and extensive qualitative results expose characteristic baseline failures rather than showing only favorable samples.

Useful applications follow from the structured latent and primitive representations, including localized inpainting, ground-conditioned object generation, outpainting, large-scale extrapolation, and instance-level editing without task-specific fine-tuning.

The paper is clear and unusually detailed. The supplement documents dataset construction, train/test separation, category mappings, object-count truncation, losses, architecture sizes, optimization, diffusion schedules, training resources, and failure cases, supporting reproducibility.

Limitations are discussed candidly, including coarse geometry, fixed semantic categories, raster-resolution constraints, missing hard geometric constraints, floating attachments, seams, and inconsistent outpainting from weak context.
weaknesses: Material evaluation weakness: all principal generation metrics are computed from top-down semantic renderings. This discards much of the vertical geometry and therefore does not adequately validate the central claim of superior 3D scene generation; no quantitative test of generated heights, collisions, object-ground support, or other physical validity is provided.

The main comparison confounds representation/model quality with conditioning. PrITTI is sampled using three vegetation-density labels, whereas every baseline is unconditional, and there is no unconditional PrITTI ablation. Uniform sampling over derived labels may change coverage and distribution matching, so the reported generation advantage cannot be attributed cleanly to the proposed representation.

Controllability and downstream editing are supported almost entirely by selected qualitative examples. There is no quantitative measurement of vegetation-condition adherence, preservation outside an inpainting mask, boundary continuity, road connectivity, or degradation over repeated extrapolation steps.

The Cholesky claim is only tested on a synthetic one-object, zero-centered, yaw-only experiment against a naive quaternion regression baseline. Quaternion sign ambiguity can be handled through canonicalization or rotation-aware losses, and established continuous rotation representations are not compared; consequently, the evidence supports this implementation choice but not a broad superiority claim.

The claimed memory advantage is based on per-scene representation size (2.52 MB), not training or inference peak memory. Model memory is especially relevant because the diffusion variants contain 130M–675M parameters. Thus, statements about lower overall memory requirements are broader than the evidence.

Reconstruction evidence is mixed: voxelized PrITTI obtains 70.27 mIoU, below XCube's 79.47 and SemCity-1M's 93.81. Moreover, object AP excludes the very frequent vegetation-ellipsoid category and lacks per-class results, while selecting the 95th-percentile query count explicitly drops objects from dense scenes.

FID, IS, precision, and recall are reported without uncertainty over training or evaluation seeds. The supplement itself demonstrates substantial sensitivity of precision/recall to sample count, reference-pose selection, and neighborhood size, making a single chosen 1K/k=3 operating point less conclusive despite the large observed margins.

There is an implementation contradiction affecting reproducibility: the main experiment section says PrITTI is evaluated without classifier-free guidance, whereas the supplement states that classifier-free guidance is used with scale 4.0. The manuscript also leaves the promised code/model URL blank.

The novelty lies primarily in representation and system integration: the VAE, DiT, DETR-style decoding, and RePaint-based manipulation are established components. This is still useful, but the manuscript should temper claims such as unlocking the 'full capabilities' of diffusion transformers and 'state-of-the-art 3D' quality given the 2D-render-based evaluation and single-dataset scope.

strengths: The hybrid representation is a meaningful and reasonably original contribution: instance-level cuboids/ellipsoids make object manipulation substantially easier than in semantic voxel grids, while raster maps accommodate irregular ground surfaces.

The method is technically coherent overall, combining a set-based VAE, spatial object latent, and diffusion transformer. The Cholesky parameterization is well motivated and evaluated against quaternions across multiple dataset sizes and seeds.

Experiments include three recent voxel-based baselines retrained on the same data. PrITTI shows large improvements in the reported generation metrics and substantially faster sampling than hierarchical alternatives.
The paper provides extensive implementation details, ablations, qualitative results, failure cases, and supplementary discussion. The presentation and figures are generally clear.
weaknesses: The principal generation evidence is not sufficiently reliable. FID, Inception Score, precision, and recall are computed by applying natural-image Inception features to top-down semantic label maps; the paper itself demonstrates that precision varies dramatically with reference sampling, sample count, and neighborhood size. No geometry-aware, semantic-validity, collision, road-connectivity, or object-placement metric corroborates the claimed quality advantage.

The comparison confounds representation and controllability. PrITTI is class-conditioned, whereas every baseline is unconditional, and the generated conditions are sampled in an equal three-way mixture without showing that this matches the reference distribution. Thus Table 3 does not isolate whether gains arise from the primitive representation, the conditional formulation, or other architecture/training differences.

The claimed controllability and downstream editing capabilities receive almost exclusively hand-selected qualitative support. There is no quantitative evaluation of vegetation-condition accuracy, preservation outside an inpainting mask, overlap consistency or seams in outpainting, ground-conditioned placement, or photorealistic synthesis. Consequently, several central claims extend beyond the supplied evidence.

The reconstruction split does not establish the asserted spatial non-overlap. Each layout spans roughly 64 m, but poses are excluded only within 5 m of the other split and test intervals have only 5 m margins. Training and test crops can therefore share substantial scene geometry, weakening reconstruction generalization conclusions.

Some comparisons and claims are overstated. The reported 2.52 MB is representation storage rather than demonstrated training/runtime memory, and the ground component remains a fixed 256x256 raster despite the claim of resolution independence. Object AP also excludes the large vegetation-ellipsoid category and averages unusually permissive IoU thresholds beginning at 0.05.

There are consequential reproducibility and correctness inconsistencies: the main text says generation evaluation uses no classifier-free guidance, while the supplement specifies guidance scale 4.0. In addition, the known-region update labeled z_(t-1) in Eq. 20 uses alpha-bar_t rather than alpha-bar_(t-1), which is inconsistent with the stated forward diffusion marginal unless this is a notation error. The public-code URL is blank.

Overall, the representation and empirical trend are promising, but the evaluation does not yet convincingly support the breadth or fairness of the main claims. These concerns are material rather than presentation-only, while the technical contribution is substantial enough to keep the recommendation near the decision boundary.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent and useful representation-level contribution: vectorized instance primitives for objects combined with rasterized ground surfaces. This directly enables instance-level translation, rotation, scaling, and deletion, capabilities that are genuinely awkward in voxel representations.

The overall system is technically well motivated. The spatial scatter-mean object encoder, disentangled ground/object latent channels, DETR-style set decoder, and latent diffusion model fit together naturally. The latent-split ablation provides meaningful support, improving AP3D from 53.78 to 62.12 and ground height MSE from 0.0355 to 0.0075.

Results on KITTI-360 are strong. Relative to the best voxel baseline, XCube, DiT-B improves precision from 0.482 to 0.712, recall from 0.230 to 0.491, and FID from 94.822 to 73.952, while reducing reported sampling time from 3.50 s to 0.58 s. Larger DiT variants further improve precision and recall.

The representation offers a favorable practical trade-off: its reported 2.52 MB scene size is below XCube's 3.05 MB and SemCity's 8.00 MB at the finest resolution, while retaining explicit object instances. The authors appropriately show that this does not dominate every reconstruction comparison: SemCity-1M obtains substantially higher voxelized mIoU, which makes the discussion more credible.

Inpainting, outpainting, ground-conditioned object generation, and direct object editing demonstrate that the structured representation has utility beyond unconditional sampling. The extensive supplement includes architecture, optimization, preprocessing, baseline-training, metric-sensitivity, qualitative-result, and failure-case details.

The manuscript is generally clear and visually effective, and it openly discusses important limitations such as coarse geometry, fixed categories, floating objects, absent collision constraints, and outpainting seams.
weaknesses: The principal quantitative generation comparison does not cleanly isolate the benefit of the representation. PrITTI uses a conditional DiT with up to 675M parameters, whereas the retrained baselines use different diffusion architectures, hierarchy designs, and unconditional objectives. Thus, the large gains cannot be attributed solely to primitives. Matched-capacity comparisons, an unconditional PrITTI result, or a voxelized DiT counterpart would materially strengthen the central claim.

Generation quality is evaluated through Inception-based metrics on color-rendered top-down semantic maps. Such natural-image features may not faithfully measure 3D semantic-layout validity, and sharp primitive boundaries can be favored over voxel outputs. The paper lacks complementary structural measures such as object-count distributions, class-conditional statistics, collision rates, road connectivity, or object-to-ground consistency.

The claimed controllability and most downstream applications are supported primarily by selected qualitative examples. There is no quantitative test of vegetation-condition adherence, preservation accuracy during inpainting, seam or connectivity quality during outpainting, or semantic consistency of the street-view synthesis. Consequently, these capabilities look promising but are less firmly established than the unconditional-generation results.

Experimental breadth is limited to one dataset and one newly constructed preprocessing/split protocol. Although KITTI-360 may be the only suitable densely annotated dataset, this leaves the claimed generality to other domains unverified. Moreover, scene windows span 64 m while train/test poses are separated using only 5 m margins, so substantial physical scene content may remain shared across reconstruction splits despite the stated goal of non-overlapping coverage.

The Cholesky study is narrow: it considers one centered vehicle with yaw-only rotations and compares against a quaternion regression susceptible to the well-known sign ambiguity. Canonicalized quaternions, sign-invariant losses, or standard continuous rotation representations are not tested. The evidence therefore supports this encoding over the particular naive quaternion baseline, but not a broad claim of superior numerical stability.

There are reproducibility inconsistencies that should be resolved. The main paper says generation uses no classifier-free guidance, while the supplement specifies guidance with scale 4.0. Also, the known-region update is denoted z_(t-1) but uses alpha-bar_t in Eq. 20, making the precise RePaint indexing ambiguous.

The fixed query counts discard objects beyond each category's 95th-percentile capacity, specifically removing the farthest instances, but the frequency and effect of this truncation are not reported. This may systematically simplify unusually dense scenes and weakens the claim that the approach naturally handles both sparse and dense layouts.
